subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: Underneath, this is a strong site. “Book Your Free Consult” is a proper booking action with a genuine offer behind it, online booking is live, Heather is identified as a doctorate-level CRNA/APRN, and named client testimonials appear through the page. That is a better foundation than most practices have.

The problem is that a first-time visitor on a phone may never see any of it. The opening screen carries an announcement bar, a pop-up form asking for full name, phone and email, a cookie consent banner, and a chat bubble — four overlays at once. The headline and the booking button are behind them. The practice's own first impression is being made by its plugins.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. This score reflects what a first-time visitor can actually reach, not the quality of the site underneath — which is considerably higher.

scorecard.finding: The headline is behind a pop-up on mobile and cannot be read.
A doctorate-level CRNA/APRN — named in About rather than near the booking.
A real booking CTA and live online booking, both obscured on arrival.
Name, phone and email are requested before anything is offered.
Four overlays compete on the first screen.
Address, phone and a considerate relocation notice all present.

strengthsLead: Almost everything below is about clearing the way to work that is already done well.

strengths.title: The call to action asks for the booking.
strengths.body: “Book Your Free Consult” names the action and removes the cost of saying yes. Many practices offer “Learn More” in that position and wonder why the diary is quiet.

strengths.title: A doctorate-level clinician is named.
strengths.body: Heather is identified as a doctorate-level CRNA/APRN. That is a high credential, clearly stated — and it is exactly the reassurance an injectables patient is looking for.

strengths.title: Online booking is live.
strengths.body: Booking runs through Aesthetic Record with a phone alternative at (860) 800-2808. A patient who decides at ten at night can act on it.

strengths.title: The relocation notice is genuinely considerate.
strengths.body: “We have moved to 225 Addison Road Suite 202! Same great complex, different suite.” That saves a returning patient a wasted trip, and it is the kind of detail that says a practice thinks about the people already on its books.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The site underneath is well built — the announcement bar, consent banner and chat widget all compete for the first screen.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. Announcement bar, a pop-up form requesting name, phone and email, a cookie banner, and a chat bubble. The headline is not visible at all.

findings.heading: Four overlays reach the patient before the practice does.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the opening screen shows: an announcement bar about the relocation; a pop-up form requesting Full Name, Phone and Email with a consent checkbox and the condition “Must spend at least $249 to claim”; a cookie consent banner across the bottom; and a chat widget reading “Hi there! Have a question? Chat with us.” The hero headline and the booking button are not visible behind them.
findings.why: Every one of these was added to help, and together they prevent the site from doing its job. A first-time visitor's opening impression of the practice is formed by four interruptions rather than by anything the practice chose to say. Some will close the tab rather than dismiss three things to find out what is offered.
findings.recommended: Let the page introduce itself first. Delay the pop-up until a visitor has scrolled or spent twenty seconds, dock the chat widget as a small closed bubble rather than an opened prompt, and keep the consent banner to a single compact line. The announcement bar can stay — it is the only one of the four earning its place on arrival.

findings.heading: The form asks for three details before offering anything.
findings.evidence: The pop-up requests Full Name, Phone and Email, with a consent checkbox agreeing to receive text messages, and states “Terms and Conditions apply. Must spend at least $249 to claim.”
findings.why: This arrives before the visitor knows what the practice does, who treats them, or what the offer actually is. Three fields and a texting consent is a large ask from a stranger, and the $249 minimum lands as a condition before the benefit has been named.
findings.recommended: Ask for the email only at this stage, and lead with what the visitor receives rather than what they must spend. Phone number and consent can be collected at booking, when the patient has already decided and giving them feels reasonable.

findings.heading: The headline is two questions long and names nothing specific.
findings.evidence: The hero reads “Ready to Radiate Confidence Inside and Out? Breathe New Life Into Your Beauty Journey”.
findings.why: Thirteen words of general beauty language, none of which name a treatment, a credential or Glastonbury. A patient comparing three practices has read a version of this on the other two, and nothing here says why this one.
findings.recommended: Name the specialism and the town, and let the credential do the persuading — a doctorate-level CRNA/APRN is a far stronger opening line than any question about radiating confidence.

findings.heading: The strongest credential is filed under About.
findings.evidence: Heather's identification as a doctorate-level CRNA/APRN appears in the About section. No credential appears in the hero or beside the booking button.
findings.why: For injectables the decisive question is who performs the treatment and what they are qualified to do. Answering it in About means answering it only for the minority who go looking.
findings.recommended: Put the name, credential and a real photograph in the hero, and repeat the credential beside the booking button. It is already true and already written — it simply needs to be where the decision happens.

findings.heading: Testimonials are published, but no rating or count.
findings.evidence: Named client testimonials from Izabella, Dianne and Lisa appear through the homepage. No star rating and no review count were visible.
findings.why: Named testimonials are good, but a visitor cannot tell whether they represent three happy patients or three hundred. A rating with a count answers the question a testimonial cannot: how many people agree.
findings.recommended: Publish the Google rating and review count near the booking button, keeping the written testimonials where they are. The two do different jobs and work best together.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: The site beneath follows convention well. The overlays are what breaks the expected experience.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: The largest, easiest tap targets on the first screen belong to a cookie banner, not to booking.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: The credential is in About and the testimonials are mid-page; neither sits beside the booking button.
A doctorate-level CRNA/APRN is a strong credential, currently placed where fewest people will read it.
On arrival a visitor faces four competing demands — form, cookies, chat, announcement — and no visible booking action.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: The free consult is a genuinely good default: it lowers the cost of the first step to nothing.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: The relocation notice reads as honest and human, and does the practice more credit than the headline does.

roadmap.actions: Delay the pop-up until scroll or twenty seconds. Collapse the chat widget to a closed bubble. Reduce the consent banner to one compact line. Reduce the pop-up to an email field and lead with the benefit rather than the $249 condition.
Move Heather's name, credential and photograph into the hero and beside the booking button. Publish the Google rating and review count. Rewrite the headline to name the specialism and Glastonbury.

Treatment-page depth with realistic expectations and candidacy notes. Post-treatment review requests to build the rating count. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). Overlays behave differently for returning visitors and for anyone who has already dismissed them, so a repeat visitor's first screen will not match the one described here.
